resources.string: Open a photo to start. Your original is never changed: edits are kept separately and can be revised at any time.
Pick a style, fine-tune the photo in the other tabs, then go back to Looks and tap “Save preset” to reuse it on other photos. Tap {icon} to compare with the original at any time.
16 bits per color, for printing or editing in another program. Files are several times larger than JPEG, and phone galleries usually cannot show them.
Keeps more saturated colors for wide-gamut screens and printing. For sharing online, sRGB is safer.
Not enough memory. Try a smaller export size.

Each photo keeps its own crop. Presets also keep each photo\'s sharpening and noise reduction.
Tap a kind of information to leave it out of the saved photo.

What the save dialog starts with. You can still change it for each photo.
Opens the system language settings for Photograin
They will appear on the home screen
Saved to Download/Photograin: Android does not accept JPEG XL among pictures
JPEG XL files go to Download/Photograin, because Android does not accept them among pictures
Enlarged with bicubic interpolation: sharper than simple stretching, but it cannot invent detail.
Limited to 48 megapixels so the photo fits in memory.
A neural network trained on photos restores plausible detail and removes compression noise. Much slower; best for small or old photos.
Get the most out of Photograin
A short guide to every feature
Choose what to do, then pick a photo.

Tap “Open photo”, or share a photo with Photograin from another app. It works with JPEG, PNG, WebP, HEIC, AVIF, JPEG XL and camera RAW files. The original is never changed: edits save themselves and come back when you reopen the photo from the recents.
Press and hold the photo to see the original, or tap {icon} to split the photo in two and drag the line between before and after. The arrows at the top undo and redo.

In the Styles tab, pick a ready-made look with one tap and set its strength. You can import .cube styles from other programs. When you like the photo, tap “Save preset” to reuse the same edits on other photos.

Exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, whites and blacks. Switch to “Curves” for finer control of the tones. Double-tap a slider\'s name to set it back to its starting value. Hold it down instead to read what that slider does.

Temperature, tint, vibrance and saturation. In “HSL” you change the hue, saturation and lightness of a single color, such as the blue of the sky. With the Eyedropper, tap something that should be white or gray and the white balance is set for you.
In Detail you set sharpness, clarity and haze, and reduce the noise of shots taken in low light. Effects adds a vignette and film grain.

Choose a ratio (1:1, 4:3, 16:9…), drag the corners, straighten the horizon, rotate or flip the photo. The perspective sliders straighten buildings and lines that lean. Auto straighten levels the photo from its lines; for something shot at an angle, use 4-point perspective: mark something rectangular and it is squared up.

From the editor menu, copy the adjustments and paste them onto another photo. For many photos at once, tap “Batch” on the home screen: apply the copied adjustments or a preset and, if you like, export them all in one go.

Tap {icon} to save a copy. Choose format, quality and size (TIFF keeps 16 bits per color): you can also enlarge the photo 2× or 4×, with AI to restore detail. The sRGB color profile is right for sharing; Display P3 and Adobe RGB keep more color for printing. Under the shooting data you choose what goes with the photo: date, camera, settings, author, location (off by default). Photo information in the ⋮ menu shows what the original contains.
With {icon} you choose where to save (Pictures/Photograin to begin with), how files are named, the default format, whether to remove the GPS location, and a light or dark theme.
Add a mask to adjust only part of the photo: linear for a sky or a foreground, radial for a subject, brush to paint exactly where you want.
Tap a mask to edit it, or drag its point on the photo.

In Retouch, Masks adjust only part of the photo. A linear gradient darkens a bright sky or lightens a foreground; a radial one brings out a subject; with the brush you paint the area yourself, and Erase fixes any overflow. Drag the points on the photo to move and shape it, use {icon} to see where it applies, and Invert to change everything else instead. Under Range a mask can be narrowed to the brightest or darkest parts, or to one color picked by tapping the photo; Whole photo with a range adjusts, say, every bright sky or every green at once.
Trace around an area: when you lift your finger it is filled, or cleared with Erase. Tap Lasso again to go back to the brush.
Paint on the photo with one finger; use two fingers to zoom.
Tap a spot, a wire or a small object to remove it. Heal blends the patch in; Clone copies it as it is.
Tap another spot to fix it. Drag a circle to move the fix, or its dashed twin to pick where the patch comes from.
Paint over what you want to remove: people, wires, writing. The AI fills it in from what is around it, on the phone.
Paint more strokes over this removal to grow it: they are filled together. Paint away from it for a new one.
Tap each red pupil: the circle fits itself to the red and turns it dark. If some red is left at the edge, make the circle larger with Brush size.

In Retouch, choose Heal and tap what you want to remove: a spot, a speck of dust, a wire. Photograin covers it with a matching nearby area. Drag the dashed circle to pick a different source, and use Clone for an exact copy. Red eye turns flash-lit pupils dark with one tap each. For larger things, such as a person or a sign, choose Remove and paint over them: the AI fills the area in.
Drag the four corners onto the edges of something that should be rectangular, such as a facade, a window or a sheet of paper.
Add a caption, a date or a signature. Drag it on the photo to place it.
Tap a text to change it, or drag it on the photo.

In Effects, Frame adds a border around the photo, or a polaroid with room for a caption. Text adds captions, dates or a signature: drag them on the photo to place them, and pick size, font and color. In Shapes you add lines, arrows, rectangles and ellipses. A text with Repeat as watermark covers the whole photo, see-through and slanted.
The subject is found by an AI model on the phone. Paint to add to it, erase to take away; use two fingers to zoom.
PNG and WebP keep the transparency; other formats get a white background.
Acts on colors like this one.
Tap the photo on the color to use.
Tap something that should be white or gray.
Add a line, an arrow or a box to point something out in the photo.
Tap a shape to edit it, or drag it on the photo.
Brightens or darkens the whole photo, like opening or closing the lens. Start here when a photo is too dark or too bright.
Pushes light and dark tones apart (more punch) or brings them together (softer, flatter look).
Acts only on the bright areas. Move left to bring back detail in a sky or a white wall.
Acts only on the dark areas. Move right to see into shadows without brightening the rest.
Sets how bright the brightest points get. Raise it for crisp whites, lower it if they look burnt.
Sets how deep the darkest points get. Lower it for rich blacks, raise it for a faded film look.
Makes the photo warmer (yellow, sunset) or cooler (blue, shade). Use it to fix light that looks off.
Shifts colors toward green or magenta. Useful under fluorescent or LED light.
Boosts dull colors more than strong ones and protects skin tones. Gentler than Saturation.
Makes every color stronger or weaker by the same amount. All the way left gives black and white.
Strengthens fine edges so details look crisper. Too much adds halos and noise.
Adds contrast to mid-sized details and textures (stone, wood, faces). Left softens them.
Removes haze and fog from landscapes and brings back depth; left adds a dreamy mist.
Smooths the grainy speckles of photos taken in low light. Too much makes surfaces look plastic.
Removes the colored blotches that appear in dark areas, without blurring detail.
Darkens the corners to draw the eye to the center; right lightens them instead.
Adds film-like grain for an analog look.
Sets how big the grain specks are: small is fine film, large is a coarse vintage look.
How thick the border around the photo is.
How big the selected text is.
How see-through the text is: lower it for a discreet signature or watermark.
Turns the text around its center.
How thick the line of the selected shape is.
Changes the shade of just this color, for example turning a yellowish green into a richer green.
Makes just this color stronger or weaker; the others stay as they are.
Makes just this color lighter or darker, for example a deeper blue sky.
How wide the brush is on the photo.
Hard gives a sharp edge to what you paint; soft fades it out gradually.
How gradually the effect fades at the edge of the area, so the change does not show.
The darkest (or first) value the mask includes.
The brightest (or last) value the mask includes.
How softly the mask fades just outside the chosen range.
How similar a color has to be to the one you picked to be included.
How strongly the chosen style or LUT is applied, from none to full.
How strongly the correction covers what is under it.
Rotates the photo by small amounts to level a tilted horizon.
Straightens lines that lean toward each other, like buildings shot from below.
Corrects a photo taken at an angle from the side, so the front looks square.
Tap a version to open it, hold it to compare it with this one.
Its edit is lost; the original photo and the other versions stay as they are.
